problemAnchor: 本节课的核心概念（Stress Definition、General Adaptation Syndrome、Stressor Sources、Stress Coping Strategies）之间有什么联系？学生在理解上最容易卡在哪里？

objective: Stress is the tension state when facing extraordinary demands, constraints, or opportunities.；Stressors originate from work, personal, and non-work life scenarios.；General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) includes three stages: alarm, resistance, exhaustion.

knowledgeNodes.name: Stress Definition
knowledgeNodes.definition: Stress refers to the tension state experienced by individuals when facing extraordinary demands, constraints or opportunities.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.

knowledgeNodes.name: General Adaptation Syndrome
knowledgeNodes.definition: The three-stage response to stress: alarm (initial reaction), resistance (coping), exhaustion (depletion of resources).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.

knowledgeNodes.name: Stressor Sources
knowledgeNodes.definition: Root causes of stress originating from work (task demands, role dynamics, interpersonal, career), personal (needs, abilities, personality), and non-work life (family, finances, personal affairs).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.

knowledgeNodes.name: Stress Coping Strategies
knowledgeNodes.definition: Daily adjustments (exercise, meditation, to-do lists, work hard then play hard), university resources (free wellness programs, gym access, counseling), and stressor classification action framework (remove, change, accept).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.

knowledgeNodes.name: Conflict Types
knowledgeNodes.definition: Four core conflict types: substantive (disagreement over rules/tasks), emotional (personality/emotion clash), functional (constructive, enhances performance), dysfunctional (destructive, hinders performance).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.

knowledgeNodes.name: Conflict Resolution Methods
knowledgeNodes.definition: Five methods: avoidance (low assertiveness, low cooperativeness), accommodation (low assertiveness, high cooperativeness), competition (high assertiveness, low cooperativeness), compromise (moderate both), collaboration (high assertiveness, high cooperativeness). Collaboration is the preferred method.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.

knowledgeNodes.name: Tuckman Team Development Model
knowledgeNodes.definition: Five sequential stages of team development: forming (initial acquaintance), storming (conflict and run-in), norming (common rule consensus), performing (efficient operation), adjourning (disbandment). Teams may revert to earlier stages due to changes.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of group dynamics.

knowledgeNodes.name: High-Performance Group Criteria
knowledgeNodes.definition: High-performance groups require shared internal norms, consistent core goals, high internal comprehensiveness, member diversity, and zero free-riding to ensure task quality.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of group dynamics.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects option B, C, or D in diagnostic question diag-boh4m-s6-0730-q1, indicating confusion between stress (feeling) and stressors (causes).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often think stress and stressors are the same thing or use the terms interchangeably, not recognizing that stress is the psychological/physical response and stressors are the triggers.

miniLesson.explain: Stress is the tension state you experience when facing extraordinary demands, constraints, or opportunities. Stressors are the specific causes that trigger that stress. For example, an upcoming IELTS exam is a stressor; the anxiety you feel about it is stress. Stressors can come from work, personal life, or non-work scenarios.
miniLesson.example: Common student stressors include IELTS requirements, homework piles, interpersonal barriers, and parental expectations. The resulting feeling of being overwhelmed is stress.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think: 'S-tress is the feeling, S-tressor is the trigger.' Stress rhymes with 'distress' (the response); stressor ends in 'or' like 'cause-or'.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is an example of a stressor? A) Feeling anxious B) A looming deadline C) Fatigue D) Irritability
guidedPractice.answer: B) A looming deadline. The deadline is the trigger (stressor); the others are stress responses.

guidedPractice.prompt: Identify whether each item is a stress or a stressor: i) worry about grades, ii) financial problems, iii) tension in shoulders, iv) noisy roommate.
guidedPractice.answer: i) stress, ii) stressor, iii) stress, iv) stressor.

guidedPractice.prompt: Maria feels her heart race and cannot focus because she has a huge group project due tomorrow and her team members are not contributing. Identify the stress and the stressor(s) in this situation.
guidedPractice.answer: Stress: heart racing, inability to focus. Stressors: the group project deadline and team members not contributing.

reteachModules.trigger: Incorrectly sequenced General Adaptation Syndrome stages (alarm, resistance, exhaustion) on diagnostic question q2.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students believe resistance occurs before alarm, or that exhaustion comes before resistance, mixing up the order of the GAS stages.

miniLesson.explain: The General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) describes how the body responds to stress in three sequential stages: alarm, resistance, exhaustion. First, the body recognizes a stressor and activates the 'fight-or-flight' response (alarm). If stress continues, the body adapts and tries to cope (resistance). Prolonged stress without relief depletes resources, leading to exhaustion and potential health problems.
miniLesson.example: Imagine a student facing final exams. Initially, they feel anxious and alert (alarm). As they study consistently, their body adapts—they feel more focused and energetic (resistance). If they keep cramming without breaks, eventually they become exhausted, get sick, or feel burnout (exhaustion).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember 'ARE' – Alarm, Resistance, Exhaustion. Think of a fire alarm (alarm), then firefighting (resistance), then firefighter collapses from exhaustion.

guidedPractice.prompt: List the three stages of General Adaptation Syndrome in correct order.
Explain why the stages must occur in the order alarm → resistance → exhaustion. What happens if the body is stuck in resistance too long?
guidedPractice.answer: The alarm stage triggers an immediate response to the stressor. If the stressor persists, the body enters resistance to cope. Prolonged resistance depletes energy, leading to exhaustion, which can cause health issues like burnout or heart disease.

guidedPractice.prompt: A manager notices that after a major project deadline, team members are irritable, sick, and low energy. Identify which GAS stage they are likely in and recommend a strategy to prevent exhaustion in future projects.
guidedPractice.answer: They are likely in the exhaustion stage. To prevent future exhaustion, the manager could set realistic deadlines, encourage breaks, and provide support resources (e.g., counseling).

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects the option 'All conflict is destructive and should be eliminated' or similar response indicating belief that all conflict is negative.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student believes all conflict is harmful and should be avoided, failing to recognize that conflict can be functional (constructive) and improve group performance.

miniLesson.explain: Not all conflict is negative. Conflict has a dual attribute: functional (constructive) conflict can enhance performance by challenging ideas, encouraging creativity, and improving decision-making. Dysfunctional (destructive) conflict hinders progress. The key is to manage conflict effectively to harness its benefits.
miniLesson.example: In a team project, two members disagree on the best marketing strategy. They debate ideas rigorously but respectfully, leading to a stronger final plan. This is functional conflict because it improves the outcome. In contrast, if they insult each other, it becomes dysfunctional.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of conflict like fire: it can cook your food (functional) or burn down your house (dysfunctional). It's not inherently bad; it depends on how you use it.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of the following is a characteristic of functional conflict? A) It reduces team performance. B) It involves personal attacks. C) It can lead to better solutions. D) It should always be avoided.
guidedPractice.answer: C) It can lead to better solutions.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the scenario: A team disagrees on a project timeline. One member suggests a tight deadline, another prefers more time. They discuss openly and agree on a moderate schedule. Is this functional or dysfunctional conflict? Explain why.
guidedPractice.answer: This is functional conflict because it is a substantive disagreement (about tasks) that leads to constructive discussion and a compromised solution, improving the team's plan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Compare two conflict situations: (1) A team argues about role assignments and ends up with clearer responsibilities. (2) A team argues because of personal dislike, leading to poor collaboration. For each, identify the conflict type (substantive/emotional) and whether it is functional or dysfunctional. Explain the impact on team performance.
guidedPractice.answer: Situation 1: Substantive conflict, functional because it clarifies roles and improves team effectiveness. Situation 2: Emotional conflict, dysfunctional because it stems from personal clashes and reduces collaboration. The difference is that functional conflict focuses on tasks and leads to better outcomes, while dysfunctional conflict focuses on people and harms performance.

reteachModules.trigger: Student answered incorrectly on diagnostic question diag-boh4m-s6-0730-q4 (collaboration vs compromise).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may think compromise is the best method because it involves give and take, but collaboration aims for a win-win solution with high assertiveness and cooperativeness.

miniLesson.explain: Collaboration and compromise are both conflict resolution methods, but they differ in assertiveness and cooperativeness. Collaboration is high in both, aiming for a win-win solution where all parties fully satisfy their interests. Compromise is moderate in both, where each party gives up something to reach a middle ground. Collaboration is more effective for complex or important issues.
miniLesson.example: Two departments disagree on a project deadline. Using collaboration, they work together to find a new deadline that meets both needs. Using compromise, they might split the difference, but neither is fully satisfied.

guidedPractice.prompt: What are the two dimensions used to categorize conflict resolution methods?
A team member is highly assertive and highly cooperative when resolving a conflict. Which method are they using?
Explain why collaboration is preferred over compromise in a business setting, using the dimensions of assertiveness and cooperativeness.
guidedPractice.answer: Collaboration achieves a win-win outcome that fully satisfies both parties' interests (high assertiveness and high cooperativeness), leading to better relationships and long-term solutions. Compromise is moderate in both dimensions, leaving each party partially unsatisfied, which may resurface later.

reteachModules.trigger: When a student answers that teams always move forward through Tuckman's stages without regression.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Assuming that Tuckman's team development stages are always sequential and progressive, and that teams never revert to earlier stages.

miniLesson.explain: Tuckman's team development model includes five stages: forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. A common misconception is that teams always move forward through these stages in a linear fashion. However, teams can and do revert to earlier stages when facing significant changes, such as resource cuts or personnel changes. For example, if a new member joins a performing team, the team might drop back to storming as they integrate the new person. Understanding this flexibility is key to managing team dynamics effectively.
miniLesson.example: A project team was performing efficiently. After a key member left and was replaced, the team struggled with roles and communication, effectively regressing to the storming stage. This illustrates that progress is not always forward.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of Tuckman as a dance, not a straight line. Sometimes you take a step back to move forward again.

guidedPractice.prompt: What are the five stages of Tuckman's team development model, and is it possible for a team to go back to an earlier stage?
guidedPractice.answer: The five stages are forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning. Yes, teams may revert to earlier stages when facing changes like resource cuts or personnel changes.

guidedPractice.prompt: A team that was in the norming stage experiences a sudden budget cut and a new manager. Which Tuckman stage are they most likely to return to, and why?
guidedPractice.answer: They are most likely to return to the storming stage because the change in resources and leadership disrupts established norms and roles, causing conflict and uncertainty.

guidedPractice.prompt: Analyze why a high-performing team might regress to an earlier stage. Provide two possible triggers and explain how the team could work to progress again.
guidedPractice.answer: Possible triggers include: (1) addition of new members, which disrupts established norms and can cause re-storming, and (2) major organizational restructuring that changes goals or resources. To progress again, the team should openly address the changes, re-establish norms through communication, and focus on rebuilding trust and collaboration, effectively moving through the stages again.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct order for the stages of General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS)?
options: Resistance, Alarm, Exhaustion
Alarm, Exhaustion, Resistance
Alarm, Resistance, Exhaustion
Exhaustion, Alarm, Resistance

questions.stem: A college student has a heavy workload for several weeks. At first, they feel anxious and have trouble sleeping (Stage 1). They then adapt, feel more focused, and manage their time well (Stage 2). Eventually, they become physically ill and cannot concentrate (Stage 3). Identify the three GAS stages in order and explain why the body moves from one stage to the next.
questions.rubric: Correctly identifies the three stages in order: alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Explanation mentions that alarm triggers an immediate stress response, resistance is the body's attempt to cope with ongoing stress, and exhaustion occurs when resources are depleted due to prolonged stress.

retestCards.passRule: Answer both questions correctly. For Q1, select option index 2. For Q2, the stages must be in the correct order (alarm, resistance, exhaustion) and the explanation must describe the progression from one stage to the next based on body's resource depletion.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations best illustrates functional conflict?
options: Team members exchange personal insults during a debate.
Two colleagues disagree on the best marketing approach, challenge each other's ideas, and ultimately develop a stronger campaign.
A manager avoids discussing a disagreement with an employee to keep peace.
A team member refuses to accept any feedback and becomes defensive.

questions.stem: Describe a real or fictional example of conflict that improved a team's performance. Identify why it was functional rather than dysfunctional.
questions.rubric: Response must include: (1) A clear conflict scenario (can be from lesson or student's own experience), (2) Explanation that the conflict focused on tasks/ideas (substantive) rather than personal attacks (emotional), (3) Statement that the conflict led to a better outcome (e.g., better solution, clearer roles, improved team cohesion). Vague or incorrect answers (e.g., saying all conflict is bad) indicate misunderstanding.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct answer for question 1, and for question 2 provide an explanation that correctly identifies functional conflict as constructive and task-focused, leading to improved outcomes. If the student repeats the misconception that all conflict is negative, they do not pass.

questions.stem: A manager is trying to resolve a conflict between two team members. She encourages both parties to express their needs fully and works with them to find a solution that satisfies everyone completely. Which conflict resolution method is she using?
options: Avoidance
Competition
Compromise
Collaboration

questions.stem: In your own words, explain the key difference between collaboration and compromise in terms of assertiveness and cooperativeness. Why is collaboration generally preferred for important conflicts?
questions.rubric: Student correctly identifies that collaboration is high assertiveness and high cooperativeness (win-win), while compromise is moderate in both (lose-lose). Student explains that collaboration aims to fully satisfy all parties, leading to better long-term outcomes, while compromise leaves everyone partially unsatisfied.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Tuckman's team development model is accurate?
options: Teams always progress linearly through forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning.
Teams may regress to earlier stages due to changes like resource cuts or new members.
Once a team reaches the performing stage, it never leaves that stage.
Regression only occurs during the adjourning stage.

questions.stem: Describe a realistic scenario in which a team that was in the norming stage might regress to an earlier stage. Explain which stage they would likely return to and why.
questions.rubric: Student identifies a specific change (e.g., new member, budget cut, leadership change) that disrupts norms/roles, explains regression to storming or forming stage, and provides reasoning involving conflict or uncertainty.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly. For the open-ended question, the response must correctly identify a trigger for regression and the likely stage (forming or storming) with a plausible explanation.

cards.question: Which statement best distinguishes stress from stressors?
options: Stress is the feeling, stressors are the causes.
Stressors are the feeling, stress is the cause.
They are the same thing.
Stress only comes from work, stressors come from personal life.
cards.diagnosis: Check whether student can differentiate the subjective feeling of stress from the external or internal triggers (stressors).
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
That's reversed. Stress is the feeling you experience; stressors are the things that cause it.
They are related but different. Stress is the response, stressors are the triggers.
Both stress and stressors can come from work, personal, and non-work life. The key difference is response vs trigger.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that stress is the feeling and stressors are the causes.
cards.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.
cards.alignmentNote: Question directly addresses stress concept, part of C2 expectation.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think stress and stressors are the same or use the terms interchangeably.

cards.question: What is the correct order of the General Adaptation Syndrome stages?
options: Alarm, Resistance, Exhaustion
Resistance, Alarm, Exhaustion
Exhaustion, Alarm, Resistance
Alarm, Exhaustion, Resistance
cards.diagnosis: Check whether student remembers the sequence of alarm, resistance, exhaustion.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
The correct order starts with alarm, then resistance, then exhaustion.
The body first reacts with alarm, not exhaustion.
Resistance comes before exhaustion. The body tries to cope before it runs out of energy.
cards.successCriteria: Student recalls the three stages in correct sequence.
cards.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.
cards.alignmentNote: GAS model is a key strategy for understanding stress response under C2.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may mix up resistance and exhaustion, or think the stages are interchangeable.

cards.question: Which of the following is true about conflict in the workplace?
options: All conflict is destructive and should be eliminated.
Conflict can be functional when it is constructive and improves group outcomes.
Conflict only occurs due to personality differences.
Emotional conflict is always beneficial because it releases tension.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that conflict has a dual attribute: functional (constructive) and dysfunctional (destructive).
misconceptions: Some conflict is functional and can improve performance.
✓ 正确
Conflict can also be substantive (over tasks/rules) and can be functional or dysfunctional.
Emotional conflict is usually dysfunctional because it involves personal clashes and hinders performance.
cards.successCriteria: Student recognizes that conflict can be functional (constructive) and not always negative.
cards.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.
cards.alignmentNote: Conflict types are part of understanding stress and conflict management under C2.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may assume all conflict is harmful and should be avoided.

cards.question: Which conflict resolution method is considered most effective because it is high in both assertiveness and cooperativeness?
options: Avoidance
Competition
Compromise
Collaboration
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can distinguish collaboration (high-high) from compromise (moderate) as the most effective method.
misconceptions: Avoidance is low in both assertiveness and cooperativeness.
Competition is high assertiveness but low cooperativeness.
Compromise is moderate in both, not high-high. Collaboration is the preferred method.
✓ 正确
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies collaboration as the preferred method, distinguishing it from compromise.
cards.ossdExpectation: Evaluate the strategies used by individuals and organizations to manage stress and conflict.
cards.alignmentNote: Conflict resolution methods are directly under C2 expectation.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think compromise is the best because it involves giving and taking, but collaboration aims for win-win.

cards.question: Which of the following best describes the Tuckman team development model?
options: Teams always move forward through the stages without going back.
Teams may revert to earlier stages when facing resource cuts or personnel changes.
The stages are: forming, storming, performing, norming, adjourning.
Once a team reaches performing, it never leaves that stage.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student knows that stages can go backward (e.g., from norming back to storming) due to changes.
misconceptions: Teams can regress to earlier stages when facing changes like resource cuts or personnel changes.
✓ 正确
The correct order is forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning. Also, the question is about progression, not order.
Teams can move back to earlier stages due to internal or external changes.
cards.successCriteria: Student understands that teams can regress to earlier stages, not always move forward.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of group dynamics.
cards.alignmentNote: Tuckman model is a key concept in group dynamics under B2.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think Tuckman's stages are linear and teams always progress forward.
